sk: यश्छन्दसामृषभो विश्वरूपः छन्दोभ्योऽध्यमृतात् संबभूव स मेन्द्रो मेधया स्पृणोतु अमृतस्य देव धारणो भूयासम् शरीरं मे विचर्षणम् जिह्वा मे मधुमत्तमा कर्णाभ्यां भूरि विश्रुवम् ब्रह्मणः कोशोऽसि मेधया पिहितः श्रुतं मे गोपाय ॐ शान्तिः शान्तिः शान्तिः ||
ro: yaḥ · chandasām · ṛṣabhaḥ · viśva-rūpaḥ · chandobhyaḥ · adhi · amṛtāt · saṁbabhūva · saḥ · me · indraḥ · medhayā · spṛṇotu · amṛtasya · deva · dhāraṇaḥ · bhūyāsam · śarīraṁ · me · vicarṣaṇam · jihvā · me · madhu-mat-tamā · karṇābhyāṁ · bhūri · viśruvam · brahmaṇaḥ · kośaḥ · asi · medhayā · pihitaḥ · śrutaṁ · me · gopāya · oṁ · śāntiḥ · śāntiḥ · śāntiḥ ||
hi: जो (यः) छन्दों (metres / वेद-मन्त्रों) का ऋषभ (bull / सर्वश्रेष्ठ) है, जो विश्वरूप (universal in form / सर्वरूप) है, जो छन्दों (Vedic hymns) से — अमृत (immortality / अमृतत्व) से — प्रकट हुआ (संबभूव) — वह इन्द्र (Lord Indra / the lord of might) मुझे मेधा (intelligence / प्रज्ञा) से स्पृणोतु (may he fill / परिपूर्ण करे)। हे देव (O God), मैं अमृत (immortality) का धारण करने वाला (bearer / धारणकर्ता) बनूँ (भूयासम्)। मेरा शरीर (body) विचर्षण (vigorous / capable / सक्षम) हो। मेरी जिह्वा (tongue) मधुमत्तमा (sweetest / अत्यन्त मधुर) हो। मेरे कर्णों (ears) से मैं बहुत (भूरि) सुनूँ (विश्रुवम्)। तू ब्रह्म (Brahman / वेद) का कोश (sheath / treasury / कोष) है — मेधा (intelligence) से आवृत (covered / ढका हुआ)। मेरे श्रुत (what I have heard / सुने हुए ज्ञान) की रक्षा करो (गोपाय)। ॐ शान्तिः शान्तिः शान्तिः।
en: He who is the bull (ṛṣabha) of the metres (chandas), who is universal in form (viśva-rūpa), who arose from the Vedic hymns, from the immortal (amṛta) — may that Indra fill me (spṛṇotu) with intelligence (medhā). O God (deva), may I become a bearer (dhāraṇa) of the immortal (amṛta). May my body (śarīra) be vigorous (vicarṣaṇa). May my tongue (jihvā) be the sweetest (madhu-mat-tamā). May I hear abundantly (bhūri viśruvam) with my ears (karṇābhyām). You are the sheath (kośa) of Brahman, covered (pihita) by intelligence (medhā). Guard (gopāya) what I have heard (śruta). Om, peace, peace, peace.

ws.e: bull / the best / the chief — ṛṣabha literally means 'bull'; used metaphorically for 'the foremost, the mightiest'; Indra is the 'bull of the metres' — the mightiest being that arose from the Vedic hymns

intelligence / retentive power / the capacity to grasp and retain knowledge — medhā is specifically the intellectual faculty that holds sacred learning; distinguished from prajñā (wisdom) and buddhi (intellect); here it is the power to absorb and retain the Veda
vigorous / capable / active — vi + √cṛṣ (to plough/move); the body should be energetic and capable, not weak or sluggish — physical fitness is a prerequisite for sustained Vedic study

sweetest / most honey-laden — madhu (honey/sweetness) + mat (possessing) + tamā (superlative); the tongue should be 'dripping with honey' — i.e., eloquent and melodious in chanting; a sweet tongue = correct and beautiful Vedic recitation

sheath / treasury / covering — kośa can mean both 'sheath' (like a sword-sheath) and 'treasury'; here the student's intellect is the 'sheath of Brahman' — the container that holds sacred knowledge; this word anticipates the famous pañca-kośa (five sheaths) doctrine of the Brahmānandavallī (2.1-5)

gr: The student's prayer for intellectual power: this mantra is a powerful prayer spoken by the student before beginning Vedic study — asking for the faculties needed to receive, retain, and transmit sacred knowledge. Structure: (1) Invocation of Indra: Indra is invoked as the 'bull of the metres' — the mightiest being born from the Vedic hymns. The student asks Indra to fill them with medhā (retentive intelligence). (2) Prayer for physical fitness: 'śarīraṁ me vicarṣaṇam' — may my body be vigorous. Vedic study requires physical stamina — long hours of chanting, memorisation, and service to the teacher. (3) Prayer for sweet speech: 'jihvā me madhumattamā' — may my tongue be the sweetest. Correct and melodious chanting. (4) Prayer for receptive hearing: 'karṇābhyāṁ bhūri viśruvam' — may I hear abundantly. The Veda is 'śruti' (that which is heard) — hearing IS the primary mode of Vedic learning. (5) 'Brahmaṇaḥ kośaḥ': 'you are the sheath of Brahman, covered by intelligence' — the student's intellect is addressed as the container of sacred knowledge. The word 'kośa' (sheath) anticipates the Brahmānandavallī's famous five-sheath (pañca-kośa) doctrine. (6) 'Śrutaṁ me gopāya': 'guard what I have heard' — a poignant request that the knowledge once received be preserved, not lost.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_1.4.1 — This mantra functions as the student's preparatory prayer — a meditation on the faculties needed for Vedic study. The invocation of Indra as 'ṛṣabha of the chandas' is significant: Indra is traditionally the deity of mental power and courage, and the chandas (metres) are the vehicles of Vedic revelation. The prayer for a vigorous body ('śarīraṁ me vicarṣaṇam') reflects the reality of gurukula education — students underwent rigorous physical discipline alongside intellectual training. The request 'śrutaṁ me gopāya' (guard what I have heard) reveals the anxiety inherent in an oral tradition — knowledge that exists only in memory can be lost. The word 'kośa' (sheath/treasury) is one of the most important terms in the Taittirīya — it will be developed into the pañca-kośa (five sheaths) doctrine in the Brahmānandavallī: annamaya, prāṇamaya, manomaya, vijñānamaya, ānandamaya. Here it appears in its simpler sense — the intellect as the 'sheath' that houses Brahman-knowledge.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — यह शिष्य की प्रार्थना (student's prayer) = अध्ययन-पूर्व (pre-study) मेधा-याचना (request for intelligence)। 'ब्रह्मणः कोशः' = बुद्धि (intellect) = ब्रह्म-ज्ञान (Brahman-knowledge) का आधार (container)। 'श्रुतं मे गोपाय' = श्रवण-ज्ञान (heard-knowledge) = सर्वाधिक मूल्यवान — उसकी रक्षा = परम आवश्यकता।
advaita.en: Shankara says this is the student's pre-study prayer — a request for intelligence. 'Brahmaṇaḥ kośa' = the intellect = the container of Brahman-knowledge. 'Śrutaṁ me gopāya' = heard-knowledge is the most precious — guarding it is the supreme necessity.
advaita.ins: Before you begin learning, pray for the tools you'll need. Ask for a sharp mind to grasp, a vigorous body to sustain, a sweet tongue to chant, and keen ears to hear. Your intellect is the sheath that will hold Brahman. Guard what enters — once heard, it must never be lost.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — इन्द्र = भगवान् का मेधा-रूप (God as intelligence)। 'स्पृणोतु' = भगवान् से मेधा-दान (gift of intelligence from God) की प्रार्थना। शरीर, जिह्वा, कर्ण = भगवद्-सेवा (service to God) के साधन — उन्हें सक्षम (capable) बनाने की विनती।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Indra = God as intelligence. 'Spṛṇotu' = prayer for the gift of intelligence from God. Body, tongue, ears = instruments of service to God — the prayer asks that they be made capable.
vishisht.ins: Ask God for intelligence — not worldly cleverness but the capacity to receive and retain His word. Your body, your tongue, your ears — all instruments of devotion. Make them fit for the Veda, and the Veda will fill them with God's own wisdom.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — इन्द्र = दिव्य मन (divine Mind) — चेतना का प्रबुद्ध रूप (illumined form of consciousness)। 'मेधा' = अन्तर्दृष्टि-शक्ति (power of insight)। शरीर-जिह्वा-कर्ण = चेतना के यन्त्र (instruments of consciousness) — दिव्य ज्ञान (divine knowledge) ग्रहण के लिए तैयार करना।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says Indra = the divine Mind — the illumined form of consciousness. 'Medhā' = the power of insight. Body, tongue, ears = instruments of consciousness — to be prepared for receiving divine knowledge.
aurobindo.ins: Indra is the divine Mind — the illuminated intelligence that grasps truth directly. The prayer asks for this divine intelligence to fill you — to make your body a fit vessel, your tongue a channel, your ears receptive. Consciousness needs prepared instruments.

dp.q: 🔍 Indra as 'ṛṣabha of the chandas' — the divine intellect
dp.a: The invocation of Indra as the 'bull (ṛṣabha) of the metres (chandas)' reveals a dimension of Indra often overshadowed by his martial exploits: Indra and intelligence: while Indra is popularly known as the warrior-god who slays Vṛtra, the Vedic tradition also associates him with mental power. The word 'indra' is etymologically connected to 'indriya' (sense-faculty) — Indra is the lord of the senses, the master of perception and cognition. Why 'bull of the metres'? The chandas (Vedic metres — gāyatrī, triṣṭubh, jagatī, etc.) are the vehicles of Vedic revelation. Each ṛṣi (seer) receives the mantra in a specific metre, and the metre carries the mantra's power. Indra is the 'bull' (mightiest, most virile) of these metres — the supreme power that emerges from the Vedic hymns themselves. The student's logic: if Indra is the mightiest intelligence born from the Vedas, then he is the ideal deity to invoke for medhā (the retentive power needed for Vedic study). The student asks the very power that the Vedas generated to help them absorb the Vedas. Connection to Bṛhadāraṇyaka: in Bṛhadāraṇyaka 5.14.4, Indra is identified with the supreme Self — 'indha iti' (he who kindles). The Kaṭha Upanishad (2.2.3) says the Self is 'no bigger than a thumb' yet 'lord of the past and the future' — this inner Indra/Self is what the student truly invokes. 'Viśva-rūpa': Indra is 'universal in form' — he pervades all the metres, all the hymns, all of reality. This epithet connects to the Gītā's viśva-rūpa-darśana (11.5-31) — the vision of the universal form.

dp.q: 🔍 'Brahmaṇaḥ kośa' — the intellect as sheath of Brahman
dp.a: The phrase 'brahmaṇaḥ kośaḥ asi medhayā pihitaḥ' ('you are the sheath of Brahman, covered by intelligence') introduces a concept that the Taittirīya will develop into its most famous teaching: 'Kośa' here: in this mantra, the student's intellect is addressed as the 'kośa' (sheath/treasury) of Brahman. The idea: sacred knowledge (Brahman/Veda) is stored INSIDE the sheath of the intellect, and medhā (intelligence) is the covering that protects it. The student prays: 'guard what I have heard' — keep the sheath intact, keep the contents safe. The pañca-kośa anticipation: in the Brahmānandavallī (chapters 2-3 of the Taittirīya), the concept of kośa will be expanded into the famous five sheaths (pañca-kośa) doctrine: (1) Annamaya kośa (food-sheath = physical body), (2) Prāṇamaya kośa (breath-sheath = vital energy), (3) Manomaya kośa (mind-sheath = mental body), (4) Vijñānamaya kośa (knowledge-sheath = intellect), (5) Ānandamaya kośa (bliss-sheath = the deepest layer). The Self (Ātman/Brahman) is nested inside all five sheaths — like a sword in its scabbard, or a treasure in its chest. The connection: here in the Śikṣāvallī, the student's intellect is ONE kośa — the container of Brahman-knowledge. In the Brahmānandavallī, this will be systematised into five nested sheaths, each deeper than the last, with Brahman at the innermost core. The seed planted here flowers there.

sk: ॐ भूर्भुवः सुवः इति वा एतास्तिस्रो व्याहृतयः तासामु ह स्मैतां चतुर्थीं माहाचमस्यः प्रवेदयते मह इति तद्ब्रह्म स आत्मा अङ्गान्यन्या देवताः भूरिति वा अयं लोकः भुव इत्यन्तरिक्षम् सुवरिति असौ लोकः मह इत्यादित्यः आदित्येन वाव सर्वे लोका महीयन्ते ||
ro: oṁ · bhūḥ · bhuvaḥ · suvaḥ · iti · vā · etāḥ · tisraḥ · vyāhṛtayaḥ · tāsām · u · ha · sma · etāṁ · caturthīṁ · māhā-camasyaḥ · pravedayate · mahaḥ · iti · tat · brahma · saḥ · ātmā · aṅgāni · anyāḥ · devatāḥ · bhūḥ · iti · vā · ayaṁ · lokaḥ · bhuvaḥ · iti · antarikṣam · suvaḥ · iti · asau · lokaḥ · mahaḥ · iti · ādityaḥ · ādityena · vāva · sarve · lokāḥ · mahīyante ||
hi: ॐ — भूः, भुवः, सुवः — ये (एताः) तीन (तिस्रः) व्याहृतियाँ (vyāhṛtis / sacred utterances / पवित्र उद्गार) हैं। इनमें से (तासाम्) एक चौथी (चतुर्थीम्) व्याहृति — माहाचमस्य (the sage Māhācamasya / ऋषि माहाचमस्य) ने प्रवेदयते (revealed / प्रकट की): 'महः' (mahaḥ / the Great / महान्)। वह (तत्) ब्रह्म (Brahman) है। वह (सः) आत्मा (the Self) है। अन्य (अन्याः) देवताएँ (deities) उसके अंग (limbs / अवयव) हैं। 'भूः' = यह लोक (this world / पृथिवी)। 'भुवः' = अन्तरिक्ष (the atmosphere / middle space)। 'सुवः' = वह लोक (that world / स्वर्ग)। 'महः' = आदित्य (the sun)। आदित्य (sun) से ही (वाव) सभी (सर्वे) लोक (worlds) महीयन्ते (are magnified / enriched / महान् बनते हैं)।
en: Om. Bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ — these indeed are the three vyāhṛtis (sacred utterances). Of these, the sage Māhācamasya revealed a fourth: 'mahaḥ' (the Great). That is Brahman. That is the Self (ātmā). The other deities are its limbs (aṅga). 'Bhūḥ' is this world (earth). 'Bhuvaḥ' is the atmosphere (antarikṣa). 'Suvaḥ' is that world (heaven). 'Mahaḥ' is the sun (āditya). By the sun indeed are all the worlds magnified (mahīyante).

ws.e: sacred utterances — vi + ā + √hṛ (to utter); the vyāhṛtis are the primordial sounds uttered by Prajāpati at creation; bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ represent the three worlds and are chanted before every Vedic recitation, especially in the Gāyatrī mantra

the sage Māhācamasya — a ṛṣi (seer) who revealed the fourth vyāhṛti 'mahaḥ'; little is known about him outside this reference; his name suggests connection to 'mahā-camasa' (great ladle — a ritual implement)

the Great / greatness — the fourth vyāhṛti, beyond bhūḥ-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ; identified with Brahman, the Self, and the sun; 'mahaḥ' is cognate with 'mahat' (the Great Principle in Sāṅkhya) and 'mahīyante' (are magnified)

limbs / parts — the other deities (devatāḥ) are the 'limbs' of Brahman; Brahman is the body, the deities are its organs; this anticipates the Puruṣa-sūkta vision where the cosmic Person's limbs become the world

ws.h: महान् बनते हैं / are magnified / are enriched
ws.e: are magnified / are enriched / become great — passive of √mah (to be great); all the worlds become great through the sun; an elegant wordplay: 'mahaḥ' (the fourth vyāhṛti) → ādityaḥ (sun) → mahīyante (magnifies) — greatness magnifies

gr: The four vyāhṛtis — from three worlds to Brahman: this mantra teaches the famous vyāhṛtis (sacred utterances) meditation. The three standard vyāhṛtis: bhūḥ (earth), bhuvaḥ (atmosphere), suvaḥ (heaven) — these are chanted daily by every Vedic practitioner, especially as part of the Gāyatrī mantra ('oṁ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, tat savitur vareṇyam...'). They represent the three cosmic planes. The fourth vyāhṛti: the sage Māhācamasya revealed a fourth — 'mahaḥ' (the Great). This fourth vyāhṛti transcends the three worlds and is identified with: (a) Brahman — the Absolute, (b) ātmā — the Self, (c) āditya — the sun. The identification chain: mahaḥ = Brahman = ātmā = āditya (sun). The other deities are 'limbs' (aṅga) of this Brahman/Self/Sun. The wordplay: mahaḥ → ādityaḥ → mahīyante: 'the Great' is the sun, and by the sun all worlds 'become great' (mahīyante). The fourth vyāhṛti embodies the principle of greatness itself. The cosmic logic: the three vyāhṛtis map the cosmos (earth, atmosphere, heaven). The fourth transcends the cosmos — it is the SUN that illumines all three worlds, just as Brahman/ātmā underlies all three planes of existence.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_1.5.1 — The vyāhṛtis are among the oldest sacred formulas in the Vedic tradition — they appear in the Ṛg Veda and are integral to the Gāyatrī mantra (Ṛg Veda 3.62.10). The three standard vyāhṛtis (bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ) are traditionally said to have been uttered by Prajāpati at creation — each utterance producing one of the three worlds. The Chāndogya Upanishad (2.23.2-3) also discusses the vyāhṛtis in connection with OM and the Sāma-veda. The sage Māhācamasya's revelation of the fourth vyāhṛti ('mahaḥ') is unique to the Taittirīya — it represents the Upanishadic move from the ritual cosmos (three worlds) to the transcendent (Brahman). The identification mahaḥ = Brahman = ātmā = āditya follows the typical Upanishadic chain of identifications (bandhu) — the macrocosmic (sun), the metaphysical (Brahman), and the microcosmic (Self) are all one. The Chāndogya (3.19.1) similarly identifies the sun with Brahman: 'ādityo brahmeti' — 'the sun is Brahman.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — तीन व्याहृतियाँ = तीन लोक (three worlds)। चौथी 'महः' = ब्रह्म = आत्मा — जो तीनों लोकों का अधिष्ठान (substratum) है। आदित्य = ब्रह्म का प्रतीक (symbol of Brahman) — जैसे सूर्य सबको प्रकाशित करता है — वैसे ब्रह्म सबका आधार। 'अंगानि अन्या देवताः' = देवता = ब्रह्म के अवयव (parts)।
advaita.en: Shankara says three vyāhṛtis = three worlds. The fourth 'mahaḥ' = Brahman = ātmā — the substratum of all three worlds. The sun = the symbol of Brahman — as the sun illumines all, so Brahman underlies all. 'The other deities are limbs' = deities = parts of Brahman.
advaita.ins: Three worlds — earth, atmosphere, heaven — mapped by three sacred sounds. But there's a fourth, beyond the three — 'mahaḥ,' the Great. That is Brahman, the Self, the Sun that magnifies everything. The three worlds are parts; the fourth is the whole.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — व्याहृतियाँ = भगवान् की सृष्टि (God's creation) के तीन स्तर। 'महः' = भगवान् स्वयं (God Himself) — जो तीनों लोकों का स्वामी (lord of all three worlds)। आदित्य = भगवान् का दृश्य रूप (visible form of God)। 'अंगानि' = समस्त देवता = भगवान् के शरीर (body of God)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says vyāhṛtis = three levels of God's creation. 'Mahaḥ' = God Himself — the lord of all three worlds. The sun = the visible form of God. 'Aṅgāni' = all deities = the body of God.
vishisht.ins: Three worlds — God's creation in three planes. The fourth utterance, 'mahaḥ,' is God Himself — above and within all three. The sun is His visible face. All the deities are His limbs. When you chant the vyāhṛtis, you're invoking the entire structure of God's cosmos.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — भूः-भुवः-सुवः = चेतना के तीन स्तर (three planes of consciousness): भौतिक (physical), प्राणिक (vital), मानसिक (mental)। 'महः' = अतिमानसिक (supramental) — चेतना का चतुर्थ स्तर — जो तीनों को अतिक्रमण (transcends) करता है। आदित्य = सत्य-चेतना (Truth-Consciousness) का प्रतीक।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says bhūḥ-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ = three planes of consciousness: physical, vital, mental. 'Mahaḥ' = the supramental — the fourth plane of consciousness that transcends all three. The sun = the symbol of Truth-Consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: Three planes of consciousness — physical (bhūḥ), vital (bhuvaḥ), mental (suvaḥ). But there's a fourth — mahaḥ, the Great, the supramental Truth-Consciousness. This is the sun that magnifies everything — not the physical sun but the light of divine Truth that illumines all planes.

dp.q: 🔍 The vyāhṛtis — from ritual formula to cosmic philosophy
dp.a: The vyāhṛtis (sacred utterances) are among the oldest and most ubiquitous elements of Vedic practice, and the Taittirīya transforms them from ritual formulas into philosophical symbols: Origin: according to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (11.1.6.3), Prajāpati (the Creator) brooded over the three worlds and 'extracted' their essences: from earth he extracted 'bhūḥ,' from atmosphere 'bhuvaḥ,' from heaven 'suvaḥ.' These three sounds are the compressed essence of the three worlds. Daily use: every Vedic practitioner chants the vyāhṛtis multiple times daily — they precede the Gāyatrī mantra ('oṁ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, tat savitur vareṇyam...'), they open every Vedic recitation, and they are chanted during the sandhyā-vandana (twilight prayers). The Taittirīya's innovation: the standard system has three vyāhṛtis for three worlds. The Taittirīya adds a FOURTH — 'mahaḥ' — revealed by the sage Māhācamasya. This fourth transcends the three worlds and is identified with Brahman/ātmā/āditya. The philosophical move: this addition mirrors the broader Upanishadic project: the Vedic ritual cosmos (three worlds, three fires, three vyāhṛtis) is not rejected but TRANSCENDED by a fourth principle that underlies the three. The three are real; the fourth is their reality. Just as OM contains a, u, m + the silence beyond (turīya), the vyāhṛtis contain bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ + mahaḥ beyond.

dp.q: 🔍 The equation: mahaḥ = Brahman = ātmā = āditya
dp.a: The identification mahaḥ = Brahman = ātmā = āditya is a compact expression of the Upanishadic worldview: Mahaḥ = Brahman: 'the Great' is not just a fourth world or plane — it IS Brahman, the Absolute. Greatness (mahat) is the nature of Brahman itself. The Kaṭha (1.2.22): 'mahāntaṁ vibhum ātmānam' — 'the Self, great and all-pervading.' Brahman = ātmā: this is THE mahāvākya (great saying) of the Upanishads in compressed form. The cosmic Absolute (Brahman) and the individual Self (ātmā) are one. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (2.5.19): 'ayam ātmā brahma' — 'this Self is Brahman.' Ātmā = āditya: the Self/Brahman is identified with the sun — not the physical sun but the sun as the principle of illumination, the source of all light and life. The Chāndogya (3.19.1): 'ādityo brahmeti' — 'the sun is Brahman.' The sun is chosen because: (a) it illumines all three worlds, (b) it is the source of all energy, (c) it is the most visible symbol of a single reality pervading everything. 'Ādityena sarve lokā mahīyante': the beautiful wordplay: 'by the sun (= mahaḥ = Brahman) all worlds become great (mahīyante).' The fourth vyāhṛti doesn't merely add a fourth world — it MAGNIFIES the other three. Brahman doesn't sit alongside the world; it makes the world what it is. 'Aṅgāni anyā devatāḥ': 'the other deities are its limbs' — all the gods are parts of this one Brahman/ātmā/āditya. This foreshadows the Puruṣa-sūkta vision and the later Vaiṣṇava theology where all devas are aṅgas (limbs) of the Supreme.

sk: भूरिति वा अग्निः भुव इति वायुः सुवरित्यादित्यः मह इति चन्द्रमाः चन्द्रमसा वाव सर्वाणि ज्योतींषि महीयन्ते भूरिति वा ऋचः भुव इति सामानि सुवरिति यजूंषि मह इति ब्रह्म ब्रह्मणा वाव सर्वे वेदा महीयन्ते ||
ro: bhūḥ · iti · vā · agniḥ · bhuvaḥ · iti · vāyuḥ · suvaḥ · iti · ādityaḥ · mahaḥ · iti · candramāḥ · candramasā · vāva · sarvāṇi · jyotīṁṣi · mahīyante · bhūḥ · iti · vā · ṛcaḥ · bhuvaḥ · iti · sāmāni · suvaḥ · iti · yajūṁṣi · mahaḥ · iti · brahma · brahmaṇā · vāva · sarve · vedāḥ · mahīyante ||
hi: 'भूः' = अग्नि (fire)। 'भुवः' = वायु (wind)। 'सुवः' = आदित्य (sun)। 'महः' = चन्द्रमा (moon)। चन्द्रमा (moon) से ही (वाव) सर्वाणि (all) ज्योतींषि (luminaries / प्रकाश-स्रोत) महीयन्ते (are magnified / महान् बनते हैं)। 'भूः' = ऋचः (Ṛg verses)। 'भुवः' = सामानि (Sāma chants)। 'सुवः' = यजूंषि (Yajur formulas)। 'महः' = ब्रह्म (Brahman / the Absolute — or OM)। ब्रह्म (Brahman) से ही सर्वे (all) वेदाः (Vedas) महीयन्ते (are magnified)।
en: 'Bhūḥ' is fire (agni). 'Bhuvaḥ' is wind (vāyu). 'Suvaḥ' is the sun (āditya). 'Mahaḥ' is the moon (candramā). By the moon indeed are all luminaries (jyotīṁṣi) magnified. 'Bhūḥ' is the Ṛg verses (ṛcaḥ). 'Bhuvaḥ' is the Sāma chants (sāmāni). 'Suvaḥ' is the Yajur formulas (yajūṁṣi). 'Mahaḥ' is Brahman. By Brahman indeed are all the Vedas magnified.

ws.e: luminaries / lights — plural of jyotis (light); here = fire, wind, sun, and the stars/planets; the moon 'magnifies' them because it reflects their light and governs their visibility (fire is more visible at night, stars shine in the moon's domain)
the Ṛg verses — ṛc = a verse of praise, especially from the Ṛg Veda; the Ṛg Veda is the oldest of the four Vedas, consisting of hymns (sūktas) composed in praise of the deities
the Sāma chants — sāman = a melodic chant; the Sāma Veda sets Ṛg Vedic verses to music; the Sāma is the Veda of melody, transforming recited verse into sung worship
the Yajur formulas — yajus = a sacrificial formula; the Yajur Veda contains the prose formulas used in ritual; the Taittirīya Upanishad itself belongs to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda tradition

the moon — candra (shining) + mā (to measure); the moon measures time (months), reflects light, and governs plant growth and tides; identified here with the fourth vyāhṛti 'mahaḥ' in the luminaries context

gr: Multiple correspondences of the vyāhṛtis: this mantra extends the vyāhṛti meditation to two more domains — luminaries and the Vedas — showing that the same four-fold structure permeates everything. Luminaries correspondence: bhūḥ = agni (fire), bhuvaḥ = vāyu (wind), suvaḥ = āditya (sun), mahaḥ = candramā (moon). Note the shift: in mantra 8, mahaḥ = āditya (sun). Here, mahaḥ = candramā (moon) while suvaḥ = āditya. The Taittirīya is not being inconsistent — it is showing that the correspondences are MULTIPLE. The same vyāhṛti can map to different realities in different contexts. Vedic correspondence: bhūḥ = ṛcaḥ (Ṛg verses), bhuvaḥ = sāmāni (Sāma chants), suvaḥ = yajūṁṣi (Yajur formulas), mahaḥ = brahma (Brahman/OM). This maps the four vyāhṛtis onto the three Vedas plus the transcendent principle. The magnification principle: 'candramasā sarvāṇi jyotīṁṣi mahīyante' — by the moon all luminaries are magnified. 'Brahmaṇā sarve vedāḥ mahīyante' — by Brahman all Vedas are magnified. In each domain, the fourth (mahaḥ) magnifies the other three — just as the sun magnified the three worlds in mantra 8.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_1.5.2 — The shifting correspondences (mahaḥ = sun in one context, = moon in another) illustrate the Vedic principle of multiple bandhu (correspondence) — the same symbol can map to different realities depending on the context of meditation. This is not confusion but richness: the vyāhṛtis are versatile symbols, not rigid labels. The three Vedas (Ṛg, Sāma, Yajur) mentioned here are the original trayi-vidyā (triple knowledge) — the Atharva Veda was a later addition to the canonical four. The Taittirīya's own lineage is the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, so the mention of yajūṁṣi carries special significance — this is the Upanishad's own Veda. The identification mahaḥ = brahma echoes the Chāndogya's treatment of OM as the essence of all the Vedas (1.1.1-9). The pattern of magnification ('mahīyante') — the fourth magnifying the three — structurally parallels the Māṇḍūkya's turīya (fourth state) that transcends and underlies waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — व्याहृतियों के बहु-स्तरीय (multi-level) अर्थ: लोक (worlds), ज्योति (luminaries), वेद (Vedas) — सबमें एक ही चतुष्क संरचना (four-fold structure)। 'महः' = सदा चतुर्थ (always the fourth) — ब्रह्म = जो सब में व्याप्त (pervades all) और सबको महान् बनाता है। तीन = विकार (modification) — चौथा = अधिष्ठान (substratum)।
advaita.en: Shankara says vyāhṛtis have multi-level meanings: worlds, luminaries, Vedas — all share the same four-fold structure. 'Mahaḥ' is always the fourth — Brahman = that which pervades and magnifies all. Three = modification — the fourth = the substratum.
advaita.ins: The same four sounds map to everything — worlds, lights, Vedas. And in every mapping, the fourth ('mahaḥ') is the one that makes the other three great. That fourth is always Brahman — the hidden ground that magnifies everything it touches.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — चार व्याहृतियाँ = भगवान् की सृष्टि के चार स्तर — हर स्तर पर भगवान् (God) = 'महः' = जो सबको महान् बनाता है। ऋक्-साम-यजुः = भगवद्-वाणी (God's speech) के तीन रूप। ब्रह्म = भगवान् — जिससे सभी वेद महान्।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says four vyāhṛtis = four levels of God's creation — at every level, God = 'mahaḥ' = the one who makes all great. Ṛg, Sāma, Yajur = three forms of God's speech. Brahman = God — by whom all Vedas are magnified.
vishisht.ins: At every level — cosmic, luminous, verbal — the same structure. And at every level, the fourth is God. Fire, wind, sun — magnified by the moon. Ṛg, Sāma, Yajur — magnified by Brahman. God is always the fourth, the one who makes everything else great.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — चार व्याहृतियाँ = चेतना के चार स्तर — भौतिक (physical = भूः), प्राणिक (vital = भुवः), मानसिक (mental = सुवः), अतिमानसिक (supramental = महः)। हर क्षेत्र में — लोक, ज्योति, वेद — वही चतुष्क (fourfold) संरचना। चौथा = सदा अतिमानसिक — सत्य-चेतना (Truth-Consciousness)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says four vyāhṛtis = four planes of consciousness — physical (bhūḥ), vital (bhuvaḥ), mental (suvaḥ), supramental (mahaḥ). In every domain — worlds, luminaries, Vedas — the same fourfold structure. The fourth = always the supramental — Truth-Consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The fourfold structure repeats in every domain. Physical, vital, mental — and the fourth, the supramental, that magnifies them all. Whether you're looking at worlds, lights, or scriptures, the pattern is the same. The fourth plane of consciousness underlies and enriches the other three.

dp.q: 🔍 Multiple correspondences — the Vedic web of meaning
dp.a: The Taittirīya's treatment of the vyāhṛtis across multiple correspondence systems illustrates a fundamental Vedic method — the construction of bandhu (cosmic correspondences): The three-plus-one pattern: in each system, three elements are mapped to bhūḥ-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, and a fourth to mahaḥ. The fourth always magnifies the three. This is the same structure as: (a) The three states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, sleep) + turīya (the fourth) in the Māṇḍūkya. (b) The three syllables of OM (a, u, m) + the silence (amātra) in the Māṇḍūkya. (c) The three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas) + the guṇa-transcendent (nirguṇa) in the Gītā. The shifting mappings: mantra 8 says mahaḥ = āditya (sun). Mantra 9 says mahaḥ = candramā (moon). This is not a contradiction but the Vedic method of multiple bandhu: the same symbolic position can be filled by different realities depending on the domain of meditation. The sun magnifies the three worlds (by illumination); the moon magnifies the three luminaries (by reflection and cyclical time). Both are valid fourth principles. Why this matters: the Taittirīya is training the student in a way of SEEING — not fixing rigid correspondences but learning to recognise the same structural pattern across every domain of experience. This is not arbitrary symbolism but a systematic method of finding unity beneath diversity.

dp.q: 🔍 The three Vedas and Brahman — speech becoming silence
dp.a: The mapping bhūḥ = Ṛg, bhuvaḥ = Sāma, suvaḥ = Yajur, mahaḥ = Brahman encodes a profound teaching about the relationship between scripture and reality: The three Vedas: (1) Ṛg Veda (ṛcaḥ — verses): the Veda of praise — hymns to the deities, recited. The oldest and most fundamental. (2) Sāma Veda (sāmāni — chants): the Veda of melody — Ṛg Vedic verses set to musical patterns. The Chāndogya Upanishad (1.1.1): 'the essence of all beings is earth; the essence of earth is water; the essence of water is plants; the essence of plants is the human being; the essence of the human being is speech; the essence of speech is the Ṛg; the essence of the Ṛg is the Sāman.' (3) Yajur Veda (yajūṁṣi — formulas): the Veda of ritual action — prose formulas guiding the performance of sacrifice. The Taittirīya Upanishad itself belongs to this Veda. Brahman as the fourth: the three Vedas are scripture — words, chants, formulas. Brahman is what they all point to — the reality beyond the words. 'Brahmaṇā sarve vedāḥ mahīyante' — by Brahman all the Vedas are magnified. Without Brahman, the Vedas would be mere sounds; with Brahman, they become vehicles of liberation. The deeper teaching: the three Vedas are like the three vyāhṛtis — they map the structured cosmos. Brahman is the fourth — the silence that gives meaning to the sound, the reality that gives power to the word.

sk: भूरिति वै प्राणः भुव इति अपानः सुवरिति व्यानः मह इत्यन्नम् अन्नेन वाव सर्वे प्राणा महीयन्ते ता वा एताश्चतस्रश्चतुर्धा चतस्रश्चतस्रो व्याहृतयः ता यो वेद स वेद ब्रह्म सर्वेऽस्मै देवा बलिमावहन्ति ||
ro: bhūḥ · iti · vai · prāṇaḥ · bhuvaḥ · iti · apānaḥ · suvaḥ · iti · vyānaḥ · mahaḥ · iti · annam · annena · vāva · sarve · prāṇāḥ · mahīyante · tāḥ · vā · etāḥ · catasraḥ · caturdhā · catasraḥ · catasraḥ · vyāhṛtayaḥ · tāḥ · yaḥ · veda · saḥ · veda · brahma · sarve · asmai · devāḥ · balim · āvahanti ||
hi: 'भूः' = प्राण (prāṇa / out-breath / प्राण-वायु)। 'भुवः' = अपान (apāna / in-breath / अपान-वायु)। 'सुवः' = व्यान (vyāna / diffused breath / व्यान-वायु)। 'महः' = अन्न (food / अन्न)। अन्न (food) से ही (वाव) सर्वे (all) प्राणाः (breaths / vital forces) महीयन्ते (are magnified / पोषित होते हैं)। ये (ताः) चार (चतस्रः) व्याहृतियाँ — चार-चार प्रकार से (चतुर्धा) — चार-चार (चतस्रः चतस्रः) हैं। जो (यः) इन्हें जानता है (वेद) — वह ब्रह्म (Brahman) को जानता है। सर्वे (all) देवाः (deities) उसे (अस्मै) बलि (tribute / offerings) लाते हैं (आवहन्ति)।
en: 'Bhūḥ' is prāṇa (the out-breath). 'Bhuvaḥ' is apāna (the in-breath). 'Suvaḥ' is vyāna (the diffused breath). 'Mahaḥ' is anna (food). By food indeed are all the vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) magnified. These four vyāhṛtis are fourfold, four by four (catasraḥ caturdhā catasraḥ catasraḥ). He who knows them — he knows Brahman. All the deities bring tribute (bali) to him.

ws.e: the out-breath / exhalation — prāṇa in its specific sense (as opposed to the generic 'life-force'); the breath that flows outward through the nostrils; one of the five vital airs (pañca-prāṇa)
the in-breath / downward breath — apa + āna; the breath that flows inward and downward; governs elimination, exhalation (in some systems), and the lower functions of the body

ws.h: व्यान-वायु / diffused breath / the pervading breath
ws.e: the diffused/pervading breath — vi + āna; the breath that circulates throughout the body; it distributes the energy of food and breath to every part; pervades the entire body like wind through a house

food — from √ad (to eat); anna is the material that sustains all the prāṇas; without food, the breaths weaken and cease; the Taittirīya elevates anna to a cosmic principle — 'annaṁ brahmeti' (food is Brahman) in Bhṛguvallī (3.2)

tribute / offering — bali = an offering made to a superior; when all deities 'bring tribute' to the knower of Brahman, it means: the cosmic forces serve the enlightened person, just as subjects serve a sovereign — knowledge of Brahman gives sovereignty over all

gr: Breaths and food — the final correspondence, and the synthesis: this mantra completes the vyāhṛti meditation with two more mappings: the vital breaths and food. The prāṇa correspondence: bhūḥ = prāṇa (out-breath), bhuvaḥ = apāna (in-breath), suvaḥ = vyāna (diffused breath), mahaḥ = anna (food). Food magnifies all the breaths — without food, the prāṇas cannot function. The synthesis: 'catasraḥ caturdhā catasraḥ catasraḥ' — the four vyāhṛtis are fourfold, four times four: (1) Worlds: earth, atmosphere, heaven, sun. (2) Elements: fire, wind, sun, moon. (3) Vedas: Ṛg, Sāma, Yajur, Brahman. (4) Breaths: prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, anna. Total: 4 vyāhṛtis × 4 contexts = 16 correspondences. The phala-śruti: 'he who knows them knows Brahman — all deities bring tribute to him.' This is the most exalted reward possible — not just personal benefit but COSMIC SOVEREIGNTY. The knower of Brahman becomes the centre to which all cosmic forces (deities) gravitate. The food-prāṇa connection: the identification mahaḥ = anna (food) is deeply characteristic of the Taittirīya. This Upanishad will develop an entire philosophy of food — from 'annaṁ brahmeti vyajānāt' (3.2) to 'annaṁ na nindyāt' (3.7-9). Food is not 'mere' matter — it is the sustainer of life, the fourth principle that magnifies the other three.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_1.5.3 — The prāṇa-correspondence (bhūḥ = prāṇa, bhuvaḥ = apāna, suvaḥ = vyāna) parallels the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's treatment of the five prāṇas (1.5.3) but uses only three of the five (omitting udāna and samāna). The identification mahaḥ = anna (food) is the first hint of the Taittirīya's distinctive emphasis on food as a cosmic principle — this will be fully developed in the Bhṛguvallī (3.1-10) where Bhṛgu's first realisation is 'annaṁ brahmeti' (food is Brahman). The formula 'catasraḥ caturdhā catasraḥ catasraḥ' (four fourfold four by four) creates a 4×4 matrix of correspondences = 16 total identifications. The claim that 'all deities bring tribute (bali)' to the knower echoes the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's powerful statement (1.4.10): 'yaḥ ātmānam eva idam upāste... tasya sarvāṇi bhūtāni ātmā eva bhavati' — for the knower of the Self, all beings become the Self.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — प्राण-अपान-व्यान = जीवन-शक्ति (life-force) के तीन प्रवाह। अन्न = चतुर्थ — जो तीनों को पोषित (nourishes) करता है। 'ब्रह्म वेद' = चार व्याहृतियों के ४×४ = १६ अर्थों को जानना = ब्रह्म-ज्ञान (Brahman-knowledge)। 'बलिम् आवहन्ति' = ब्रह्मज्ञानी = सर्वाधिपति (sovereign over all)।
advaita.en: Shankara says prāṇa-apāna-vyāna = three streams of life-force. Anna (food) = the fourth that nourishes all three. 'Knowing Brahman' = knowing the 4×4 = 16 correspondences of the vyāhṛtis = Brahman-knowledge. 'Deities bring tribute' = the knower of Brahman = sovereign over all.
advaita.ins: The final mapping: three breaths sustained by food. And with this, the full picture: 4 vyāhṛtis × 4 domains = 16 cosmic correspondences. Know them all, and you know Brahman. Know Brahman, and every force in the cosmos serves you — not because you command, but because you understand.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — प्राण-वायुएँ = भगवान् की जीवन-शक्ति (God's life-force) शरीर में। अन्न = भगवान् का अन्न-रूप (God as food) — जो सबको पोषित करता है। ४×४ व्याहृतियाँ = भगवान् की सृष्टि का सम्पूर्ण मानचित्र (complete map of God's creation)। जानने वाला = भगवत्-कृपा-पात्र (recipient of God's grace)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the vital breaths = God's life-force in the body. Food = God as food — who nourishes all. The 4×4 vyāhṛtis = the complete map of God's creation. The knower = the recipient of God's grace.
vishisht.ins: God sustains you as food, breathes in you as prāṇa, and magnifies everything through His presence. The four vyāhṛtis in four domains — that's the complete map of His creation. Know the map, know the Creator, and all creation serves you through His grace.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — प्राण-अपान-व्यान = चेतना-शक्ति (consciousness-force) के तीन प्रवाह: ऊर्ध्व (ascending), अधो (descending), व्यापक (diffusing)। अन्न = भौतिक आधार (material base) — चेतना को शरीर में स्थापित रखने वाला। ४×४ = चेतना का सम्पूर्ण मानचित्र (complete map of consciousness)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says prāṇa-apāna-vyāna = three flows of consciousness-force: ascending, descending, and diffusing. Food = the material base that anchors consciousness in the body. 4×4 = the complete map of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: Three currents of life-force — ascending, descending, pervading — sustained by food, the material anchor. The four vyāhṛtis in four domains give you the complete map of consciousness at every level. Master that map, and consciousness itself serves you — all forces become your tributaries.

dp.q: 🔍 Anna (food) as the fourth principle — the Taittirīya's distinctive teaching
dp.a: The identification mahaḥ = anna (food) in the prāṇa-context introduces what will become the Taittirīya's most distinctive philosophical contribution — the elevation of food to a cosmic and spiritual principle: Why food? In the prāṇa-mapping, the three breaths (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna) are the life-forces that animate the body. But without food, the breaths weaken and die. Food is the MATERIAL BASIS of all life-force. It is the fourth principle that 'magnifies' the other three — just as Brahman magnifies the three Vedas, and the sun magnifies the three worlds. The Taittirīya's food philosophy: this theme will be developed through the rest of the Upanishad: (a) Brahmānandavallī 2.2: 'From food (anna) indeed are all beings born; having been born, by food they live; departing, into food they enter.' (b) Bhṛguvallī 3.2: 'annaṁ brahmeti vyajānāt' — Bhṛgu's first realisation: 'food is Brahman.' (c) Bhṛguvallī 3.7-10: 'annaṁ na nindyāt' — 'do not despise food'; 'annaṁ na paricakṣīta' — 'do not reject food'; 'annaṁ bahu kurvīta' — 'make food abundant.' The philosophical implication: the Taittirīya refuses to treat matter/food as 'low' or 'unspiritual.' Food is not the opposite of spirit — it is spirit's material foundation. This is a remarkably life-affirming, world-affirming teaching — the sacred and the material are not at war but in a relationship of mutual sustenance. The body needs food; the soul expresses itself through the body; therefore food is sacred.

dp.q: 🔍 The 4×4 matrix — cosmic sovereignty through knowledge
dp.a: The synthesis 'catasraḥ caturdhā catasraḥ catasraḥ' (four fourfold, four by four) reveals the Taittirīya's systematic approach to cosmic knowledge: The complete matrix: 4 vyāhṛtis × 4 domains = 16 correspondences: (1) Worlds: bhūḥ = earth, bhuvaḥ = atmosphere, suvaḥ = heaven, mahaḥ = sun. (2) Elements: bhūḥ = fire, bhuvaḥ = wind, suvaḥ = sun, mahaḥ = moon. (3) Vedas: bhūḥ = Ṛg, bhuvaḥ = Sāma, suvaḥ = Yajur, mahaḥ = Brahman. (4) Breaths: bhūḥ = prāṇa, bhuvaḥ = apāna, suvaḥ = vyāna, mahaḥ = food. The teaching method: the student is asked to hold ALL 16 correspondences simultaneously — to see that when they chant 'bhūḥ,' they are invoking earth AND fire AND Ṛg Veda AND prāṇa all at once. The single syllable contains four realities. The reward: cosmic sovereignty: 'sarve asmai devāḥ balim āvahanti' — all deities bring tribute to the knower. This is the Upanishadic concept of jñāna-phala (the fruit of knowledge): knowledge doesn't just inform — it transforms. The knower of the 16 correspondences becomes a 'junction point' (cf. the saṁhitā meditation) where all cosmic forces converge. The deities don't serve the knower out of submission but because the knower has BECOME the centre of the cosmic web — understanding the connections makes you the connection.

sk: ॐ इति ब्रह्म ॐ इतीदꣳ सर्वम् ॐ इत्येतदनुकृतिर्ह स्म वा अप्यो श्रावयेत्याश्रावयन्ति ॐ इति सामानि गायन्ति ॐ शोम् इति शस्त्राणि शꣳसन्ति ॐ इत्यध्वर्युः प्रतिगरं प्रतिगृणाति ॐ इति ब्रह्मा प्रसौति ॐ इत्यग्निहोत्रमनुजानाति ॐ इति ब्राह्मणः प्रवक्ष्यन्नाह ब्रह्मोपाप्नवानीति ब्रह्मैवोपाप्नोति ||

hi: ॐ = ब्रह्म (Brahman)। ॐ = यह सब (idaṁ sarvam / this entire [universe])। ॐ — यह (एतत्) अनुकृति (imitation / अनुकरण / approval) का शब्द है — 'ॐ श्रावय' (OM, make [them] hear) — इस प्रकार (इति) आश्रावयन्ति (they make [the gods] hear / वे सुनवाते हैं)। ॐ — इस प्रकार (इति) सामानि (Sāma chants) गायन्ति (they sing / गाते हैं)। 'ॐ शोम्' — इस प्रकार (इति) शस्त्राणि (the śastra recitations) शंसन्ति (they recite / पढ़ते हैं)। ॐ — इस प्रकार अध्वर्यु (the Yajur-priest / यजुर्-पुरोहित) प्रतिगर (response / प्रत्युत्तर) प्रतिगृणाति (responds / देता है)। ॐ — इस प्रकार ब्रह्मा (the Brahman-priest / ब्रह्मा-पुरोहित) प्रसौति (gives permission / अनुमति देता है)। ॐ — इस प्रकार अग्निहोत्र (the fire-offering) को अनुजानाति (one permits / अनुमति देता है)। ॐ — इस प्रकार ब्राह्मण (a Brahmin / ब्राह्मण) प्रवक्ष्यन् (about to recite / पढ़ने वाला) आह (says / कहता है): 'ब्रह्म उपाप्नवानि' (may I attain Brahman / मैं ब्रह्म प्राप्त करूँ)। ब्रह्म एव (Brahman itself / ब्रह्म ही) उपाप्नोति (he attains / प्राप्त करता है)।
en: OM is Brahman. OM is this entire universe (idaṁ sarvam). OM — this is [the syllable of] compliance (anukṛti): when they say 'OM, śrāvaya' ('make them hear'), they make the gods hear. With OM they sing the Sāma chants. With 'OM, śom' they recite the śastra recitations. With OM the adhvaryu priest gives the response (pratigara). With OM the Brahman-priest gives permission (prasauti). With OM one permits the agnihotra (fire-offering). With OM a Brahmin about to recite (pravakṣyan) says: 'May I attain Brahman (brahma upāpnavāni).' He attains Brahman indeed (brahma eva upāpnoti).

ws.e: compliance / imitation / approval — anu + √kṛ (to do after/following); OM is the sound of assent, of compliance — when someone says 'OM,' they are affirming, agreeing, permitting; it is the verbal seal of approval in Vedic ritual
the Yajur priest — the adhvaryu is the priest who performs the physical actions of the sacrifice and recites the Yajur Veda formulas; one of the four main priests (hotṛ, adhvaryu, udgātṛ, brahmā)

ws.h: ब्रह्मा-पुरोहित / the Brahman-priest / the supervising priest
ws.e: the Brahman-priest — the silent supervisor of the sacrifice who oversees the entire ritual; sits quietly and intervenes only to correct errors; represents the totality of Vedic knowledge; NOT Brahmā the creator-god
the fire-offering — the daily oblation into the sacred fire, performed at dawn and dusk; the most basic and universal Vedic ritual; maintained by the householder throughout life

attains / obtains — upa + √āp (to reach/attain); the one who says OM with the intention of attaining Brahman DOES attain Brahman; the intention (saṅkalpa) combined with the sacred syllable produces the result

gr: OM in Vedic ritual and as Brahman: this mantra is a comprehensive survey of OM's role across the entire Vedic ritual system and its ultimate identification with Brahman. The opening declarations: (1) 'OM is Brahman' — OM IS the Absolute, not merely a symbol of it. (2) 'OM is this entire universe' — OM encompasses all reality. These echo the Māṇḍūkya Upanishad (1): 'oṁ ity etad akṣaram idaṁ sarvam.' OM in ritual: the mantra then surveys every major ritual function where OM is used: (a) The Hotṛ priest's call: 'OM śrāvaya' — make the gods hear. (b) The Udgātṛ priest: 'OM iti sāmāni gāyanti' — Sāma chants begin with OM. (c) The Hotṛ's śastra recitation: 'OM śom iti śastrāṇi śaṁsanti.' (d) The Adhvaryu's response: 'OM iti pratigaram pratigṛṇāti.' (e) The Brahmā priest's permission: 'OM iti prasauti.' (f) The agnihotra: 'OM iti anujānāti.' The culmination: a Brahmin about to recite says 'OM — may I attain Brahman.' And the text declares: 'brahma eva upāpnoti' — he attains Brahman INDEED. The intention (saṅkalpa) plus the syllable (OM) produces the result. The philosophical point: OM pervades every layer of Vedic practice — from the most elaborate śrauta ritual to the simplest daily offering. It is the one syllable common to all. And it IS Brahman — so every ritual use of OM is already a contact with the Absolute.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_1.8.1 — This mantra parallels the Chāndogya's treatment of OM (1.1.1-9) and the Māṇḍūkya's opening declaration ('oṁ ity etad akṣaram idaṁ sarvam'). The survey of OM's ritual uses covers the four main Vedic priests: (1) Hotṛ — who recites the Ṛg Veda (the 'śrāvaya' call and śastra recitations), (2) Udgātṛ — who sings the Sāma Veda ('sāmāni gāyanti'), (3) Adhvaryu — who performs the Yajur Veda actions ('pratigaram pratigṛṇāti'), (4) Brahmā — who supervises silently ('prasauti'). The four priests represent the four Vedas in action. OM is the thread running through all four — the one syllable that unifies all Vedic activity. The phrase 'brahma upāpnavāni... brahma eva upāpnoti' (may I attain Brahman... he attains Brahman indeed) expresses the Upanishadic confidence in the power of knowledge-cum-intention: to know what OM is and to use it with the right intention IS to attain Brahman.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — ॐ = ब्रह्म = सम्पूर्ण विश्व। ॐ = 'अनुकृति' (compliance) — यज्ञ (sacrifice) के प्रत्येक चरण में ॐ = स्वीकृति (acceptance)। 'ब्रह्म उपाप्नवानि' = ब्रह्म-प्राप्ति की अभिलाषा (desire to attain Brahman) + ॐ = ब्रह्म-प्राप्ति ही (attainment of Brahman)। ज्ञान + संकल्प = मोक्ष।
advaita.en: Shankara says OM = Brahman = the entire universe. OM = compliance (anukṛti) — at every step of the sacrifice, OM = acceptance. 'May I attain Brahman' — the desire for Brahman + OM = attainment of Brahman. Knowledge + intention = liberation.
advaita.ins: OM is everywhere in Vedic practice — every call, every chant, every permission, every response. It's not decoration — it IS Brahman. When the Brahmin says 'May I attain Brahman' with OM, the text says simply: he attains it. The syllable is the destination.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — ॐ = भगवान् का नाम-रूप (God's name-form)। यज्ञ के प्रत्येक कर्म में ॐ = भगवान् का आह्वान (invocation of God)। 'ब्रह्म उपाप्नोति' = ॐ + भक्ति (devotion) = भगवत्-प्राप्ति (attainment of God)। ॐ = भगवान् तक पहुँचने का सेतु (bridge to God)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says OM = God's name-form. In every ritual action, OM = invocation of God. 'He attains Brahman' = OM + devotion = attainment of God. OM = the bridge to God.
vishisht.ins: Every time a priest says OM in the ritual, he's invoking God. The Sāma singer, the Yajur performer, the supervisor, the fire-offerer — all use OM, all touch God through it. Say OM with the intention of reaching God, and you reach Him. The syllable is the bridge.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — ॐ = चेतना का बीज-मन्त्र (seed-mantra of consciousness)। 'इदं सर्वम्' = ॐ = सम्पूर्ण अस्तित्व (entire existence) — ध्वनि-रूप में। यज्ञ में ॐ = चेतना की क्रियाशीलता (consciousness in action)। 'ब्रह्म उपाप्नोति' = ॐ के माध्यम से चेतना = ब्रह्म-चेतना (Brahman-consciousness) तक पहुँचती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says OM = the seed-mantra of consciousness. 'Idaṁ sarvam' = OM = the entire existence in the form of sound. In ritual, OM = consciousness in action. 'He attains Brahman' = through OM, consciousness reaches Brahman-consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: OM is consciousness compressed into a single syllable — and that syllable contains the entire universe. Every ritual use of OM is consciousness acting through sound. When you say OM with the intention of reaching the Absolute, consciousness returns to its source. The seed-sound unfolds into the infinite.

dp.q: 🔍 OM across the four Vedic priests — the unifying thread
dp.a: The mantra's survey of OM's uses across the four main Vedic priests reveals OM as the thread that unifies all Vedic activity: The four priests and their Vedas: (1) Hotṛ (Ṛg Veda): the reciter — calls out 'OM śrāvaya' to begin the ritual; recites the śastra (laudatory hymns) with 'OM śom.' The Hotṛ's role is INVOCATION — calling the gods to the sacrifice. (2) Udgātṛ (Sāma Veda): the singer — 'sāmāni gāyanti' — sings the Sāma chants beginning with OM. The Udgātṛ's role is PRAISE through melody. (3) Adhvaryu (Yajur Veda): the performer — gives the pratigara (ritual response) with OM. The Adhvaryu performs the physical actions of the sacrifice — pouring oblations, arranging implements. (4) Brahmā (Atharva Veda / all Vedas): the silent supervisor — gives permission (prasauti) with OM. The Brahmā sits silently observing the entire ritual, intervening only to correct errors. Represents the TOTALITY of Vedic knowledge. OM as the common thread: each priest uses a different Veda, performs a different function, but ALL use OM. OM is the one syllable that cuts across all divisions — all Vedas, all priestly functions, all ritual stages. The culmination: after surveying OM in all its ritual uses, the text moves to the individual: a Brahmin about to study says OM and declares 'may I attain Brahman.' The shift from ritual to personal aspiration is seamless — because OM works at both levels.

dp.q: 🔍 'Brahma upāpnavāni — brahma eva upāpnoti' — intention and attainment
dp.a: The closing declaration 'brahma upāpnavāni... brahma eva upāpnoti' (may I attain Brahman... he attains Brahman indeed) encapsulates a core Upanishadic teaching about the power of knowledge combined with intention: The mechanism: the Brahmin says OM and declares his intention: 'may I attain Brahman.' The text responds: 'he attains Brahman indeed (eva).' The 'eva' (indeed/certainly) is emphatic — there is no doubt, no maybe. The attainment is assured. Why does it work? (1) OM IS Brahman: the mantra has already declared 'oṁ iti brahma.' So when the Brahmin says OM, he is already in contact with Brahman. The attainment is not a future event — it is a present recognition. (2) Intention (saṅkalpa): the Brahmin's declaration 'may I attain Brahman' is not a wish but a saṅkalpa — a solemn intention. In Vedic thought, saṅkalpa (directed will) is a creative force. Combined with the right knowledge (that OM = Brahman) and the right action (utterance of OM), it produces the result. (3) Knowledge transforms: the Upanishadic principle — 'ya evaṁ veda' (he who knows thus) — knowledge is not passive information but active transformation. To truly KNOW that OM is Brahman is to BE in Brahman. The knowing IS the attaining. The practical teaching: before beginning any recitation or study, say OM with full awareness that (a) OM is Brahman, and (b) your intention is to reach Brahman. The syllable + the knowledge + the intention = the attainment. Nothing else is needed.

sk: ऋतं च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च सत्यं च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च तपश्च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च दमश्च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च शमश्च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च अग्नयश्च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च अग्निहोत्रं च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च अतिथयश्च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च मानुषं च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च प्रजा च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च प्रजनश्च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च प्रजातिश्च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च सत्यमिति सत्यवचा राथीतरः तप इति तपोनित्यः पौरुशिष्टिः स्वाध्यायप्रवचने एवेति नाको मौद्गल्यः तद्धि तपस्तद्धि तपः ||

hi: ऋत (cosmic truth / ऋत) और (च) स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन (self-study and teaching / स्वाध्याय और प्रवचन)। सत्य (truth / सत्य) और स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन। तपस् (austerity / तप) और स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन। दम (sense-control / इन्द्रिय-दमन) और स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन। शम (tranquility / शान्ति) और स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन। अग्नि (the sacred fires / अग्नियाँ) और स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन। अग्निहोत्र (the fire-offering) और स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन। अतिथि (guests / अतिथि-सत्कार) और स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन। मानुषम् (human conduct / मानवता / humaneness) और स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन। प्रजा (progeny / सन्तान) और स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन। प्रजनः (procreation) और स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन। प्रजातिः (propagation / वंश-वृद्धि) और स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन। 'सत्यम्' (truth alone) — इति (thus says) सत्यवचा राथीतर (Satyavacā Rāthītara / सत्यवादी ऋषि राथीतर)। 'तपः' (austerity alone) — इति (thus says) तपोनित्य पौरुशिष्टि (Taponityā Pauruśiṣṭi / नित्य-तपस्वी ऋषि पौरुशिष्टि)। 'स्वाध्यायप्रवचने एव' (self-study and teaching alone) — इति (thus says) नाक मौद्गल्य (Nāka Maudgalya / ऋषि नाक मौद्गल्य) — क्योंकि वही (तत् हि) तप (austerity) है, वही तप है।
en: Cosmic truth (ṛta) and self-study and teaching (svādhyāya-pravacana). Truth (satya) and self-study and teaching. Austerity (tapas) and self-study and teaching. Sense-control (dama) and self-study and teaching. Tranquility (śama) and self-study and teaching. The sacred fires (agni) and self-study and teaching. The fire-offering (agnihotra) and self-study and teaching. Hospitality to guests (atithi) and self-study and teaching. Human conduct (mānuṣa) and self-study and teaching. Progeny (prajā) and self-study and teaching. Procreation (prajana) and self-study and teaching. Propagation (prajāti) and self-study and teaching. 'Truth [is supreme]' — thus says Satyavacā Rāthītara. 'Austerity [is supreme]' — thus says Taponityā Pauruśiṣṭi. 'Self-study and teaching alone' — thus says Nāka Maudgalya — for THAT indeed is austerity, THAT indeed is austerity.

ws.h: स्वाध्याय और प्रवचन / self-study and teaching
ws.e: self-study and teaching — svādhyāya (sva + adhyāya = one's own study = personal recitation/study of the Veda) + pravacana (teaching/expounding to others); the compound represents the complete cycle of knowledge: receiving it (svādhyāya) and transmitting it (pravacana)
cosmic truth / cosmic order — the objective order of reality (cf. mantra 1 where the student vows to speak ṛta); here listed as one of the duties that coexists with svādhyāya-pravacana

sense-control / external restraint — from √dam (to tame/subdue); control over the senses (eyes, ears, tongue, etc.); distinguished from śama (inner tranquility); dama = outer restraint, śama = inner peace
tranquility / inner peace — from √śam (to be calm); the calming of the mind's agitation; distinguished from dama (sense-control); śama is internal, dama is external — both are needed alongside study

ws.h: मानवता / मानवीय आचरण / human conduct / humaneness
ws.e: human conduct / humaneness — from manuṣya (human being); the discharge of human social duties — conduct appropriate to a human being living in society; often interpreted as ordinary worldly duties that must not be neglected for the sake of study

gr: The great litany of duties — svādhyāya-pravacana as the constant: this mantra is one of the most remarkable passages in the Upanishads — a rhythmic litany that pairs every conceivable duty with the refrain 'and self-study and teaching' (svādhyāya-pravacane ca). The structure: twelve duties are listed, each paired with svādhyāya-pravacana: (1) ṛta (cosmic truth), (2) satya (truth), (3) tapas (austerity), (4) dama (sense-control), (5) śama (tranquility), (6) agni (sacred fires), (7) agnihotra (fire-offering), (8) atithi (hospitality), (9) mānuṣa (human conduct), (10) prajā (progeny), (11) prajana (procreation), (12) prajāti (propagation). The teaching: no matter what other duties you fulfil — truth, austerity, ritual, family, social — svādhyāya-pravacana must ALWAYS accompany them. Study and teaching are not alternatives to life's duties; they are the constant thread running through ALL of them. The three sages: three teachers give their verdicts on what is most important: (a) Satyavacā Rāthītara: 'satya' (truth) is supreme. (b) Taponityā Pauruśiṣṭi: 'tapas' (austerity) is supreme. (c) Nāka Maudgalya: 'svādhyāya-pravacana alone' — because THAT is the real tapas. The resolution: the text gives the last word to Nāka Maudgalya — self-study and teaching IS the highest austerity ('tat hi tapaḥ, tat hi tapaḥ'). The emphatic repetition seals it: study and teaching are not just ONE duty among many — they ARE tapas itself.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_1.9.1 — This mantra has been called the Taittirīya's 'creed' — a comprehensive statement of the values that should govern a Vedic student's and householder's life. The refrain 'svādhyāya-pravacane ca' (and self-study and teaching) appears after EVERY other duty, making it the one non-negotiable. The twelve duties span the entire range of Vedic life: from the most abstract (ṛta, satya) through the spiritual (tapas, dama, śama) to the ritual (agni, agnihotra) and the social/biological (atithi, mānuṣa, prajā, prajana, prajāti). The three sages who offer their opinions represent three legitimate emphases within the tradition: truth (satya), austerity (tapas), and study (svādhyāya). The text's endorsement of Nāka Maudgalya's position — that svādhyāya-pravacana IS tapas — reflects the Taittirīya school's deep commitment to the continuity of the oral tradition. The emphatic 'tat hi tapaḥ, tat hi tapaḥ' (that indeed is tapas, that indeed is tapas) is a rare double affirmation — the repetition signals supreme importance.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — बारह कर्तव्य = गृहस्थ-जीवन (householder life) का सम्पूर्ण विधान (complete code)। स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन = सबका सूत्र (thread of all) — कोई भी कर्तव्य बिना अध्ययन के अधूरा। नाक मौद्गल्य = सर्वश्रेष्ठ मत (best opinion) — स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन = परम तप (supreme austerity) — क्योंकि ज्ञान = मोक्ष का एकमात्र साधन।
advaita.en: Shankara says twelve duties = the complete code of householder life. Svādhyāya-pravacana = the thread running through all — no duty is complete without study. Nāka Maudgalya's verdict is supreme — self-study and teaching = the highest austerity — because knowledge = the sole means to liberation.
advaita.ins: Twelve duties — from cosmic truth to procreation — and through every one of them runs a single thread: study and teach. Whatever else you do — maintain fires, welcome guests, raise children — never stop studying and never stop teaching. That IS the highest tapas. The text says it twice.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — बारह कर्तव्य = भगवद्-सेवा (service to God) के बारह आयाम। स्वाध्याय = भगवद्-वचन (God's word) का अध्ययन — प्रवचन = उसका प्रसार (spreading)। नाक मौद्गल्य = भगवद्-वचन का अध्ययन और प्रसार = सर्वोच्च तप — क्योंकि यही भगवान् को सबसे प्रिय (most dear to God)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says twelve duties = twelve dimensions of service to God. Svādhyāya = study of God's word — pravacana = spreading it. Nāka Maudgalya says studying and teaching God's word = the highest austerity — because this is most dear to God.
vishisht.ins: All twelve duties are forms of service to God. But the one that must never stop — the thread through everything — is studying God's word and teaching it. Truth matters, austerity matters, fires matter, guests matter, children matter. But study and teaching IS the tapas that makes all the rest meaningful.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — बारह कर्तव्य = मानव-चेतना (human consciousness) के बारह अभ्यास-क्षेत्र (fields of practice)। स्वाध्याय-प्रवचन = चेतना का आत्म-विकास (self-development of consciousness) + दूसरों तक संचरण (transmission to others)। यह = सर्वोच्च तप — क्योंकि चेतना का विकास = अस्तित्व का परम उद्देश्य (supreme purpose of existence)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says twelve duties = twelve fields of practice for human consciousness. Svādhyāya-pravacana = the self-development of consciousness + its transmission to others. This = the highest austerity — because the development of consciousness = the supreme purpose of existence.
aurobindo.ins: Every duty listed — truth, austerity, control, ritual, family, society — is a field where consciousness develops. But study and teaching is the practice that runs through all of them — the continuous self-development AND transmission of consciousness. That's the real tapas — not deprivation but growth.

dp.q: 🔍 The three sages — three views on the highest duty
dp.a: The debate among three named sages about what matters most is a characteristic Upanishadic device — presenting multiple views before offering a resolution: Satyavacā Rāthītara: 'Truth is supreme': his very NAME means 'truth-speaker' (satya-vacas) — his identity is his teaching. For him, truth (satya) is the foundation of everything: without truth, study is empty, austerity is pretence, and ritual is mechanical. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (5.5.1) confirms: 'satyaṁ vai brahma' — truth is indeed Brahman. Taponityā Pauruśiṣṭi: 'Austerity is supreme': his name means 'ever-engaged in tapas' (tapo-nitya). For him, tapas (intense discipline/austerity) is the master practice — truth without the fire of tapas remains theoretical, study without discipline is dilettantism. The Muṇḍaka (1.2.11) confirms: tapas is one of the prerequisites for Brahman-knowledge. Nāka Maudgalya: 'Self-study and teaching alone': he receives the emphatic final word: 'svādhyāya-pravacane eva' — study and teaching ALONE (eva). His clincher: 'tat hi tapaḥ, tat hi tapaḥ' — study and teaching IS tapas. He doesn't reject truth or austerity — he says study CONTAINS them. Honest study requires truth; disciplined study IS austerity. The resolution: the text endorses Nāka Maudgalya — not because truth and tapas don't matter, but because svādhyāya-pravacana includes and transcends both. Study that is honest IS satya. Study that is disciplined IS tapas. And study that is transmitted (pravacana) ensures the tradition survives. The Taittirīya's identity: this endorsement defines the Taittirīya school — a lineage that values the CONTINUITY of the oral tradition above all else. This leads directly to the convocation address (1.11), which will charge the departing student to carry the tradition forward.

dp.q: 🔍 Svādhyāya-pravacana — the cycle of learning and teaching
dp.a: The compound svādhyāya-pravacana (self-study and teaching) describes a CYCLE, not two separate activities: Svādhyāya (self-study): sva (one's own) + adhyāya (study/recitation) = personal study of the Vedic texts. This includes: (a) Recitation: daily chanting of one's own Vedic branch — maintaining the text in memory through regular repetition. (b) Study: deepening understanding through reflection, discussion with the teacher, and meditation on the meaning. (c) Self-examination: the 'sva' (self) element — studying not just texts but oneself through the texts. Pravacana (teaching): pra (forth) + √vac (to speak) = teaching/expounding to others. This includes: (a) Formal teaching: transmitting the Vedic texts to students in the gurukula. (b) Public discourse: explaining the Vedic teachings to the broader community. (c) Living the teaching: embodying what one has studied — teaching by example as much as by word. Why the compound is inseparable: svādhyāya without pravacana = knowledge hoarded, tradition dying. Pravacana without svādhyāya = teaching without depth, transmission without substance. The two together form a cycle: study → teach → deeper study → deeper teaching. Each act of teaching reveals gaps in understanding, prompting further study. Each round of study provides new insights to teach. The connection to tapas: Nāka Maudgalya's claim that svādhyāya-pravacana IS tapas makes sense through this lens: maintaining this cycle requires immense discipline (tapas) — daily recitation, constant refinement of understanding, patience in teaching, humility in learning. The austerity of the scholar is as demanding as the austerity of the forest-dweller — just differently directed.
